It also calls for reviews of job training programs and asks agencies to identify programs that are ineffective, redundant, or unnecessary.

13802.s: This executive order changes an earlier order about visa and foreign visitor processing goals and the Task Force on Travel and Competitiveness. It deletes one part of that earlier order and tells the Secretaries of State and Homeland Security to revise the implementation plan as needed. It applies to the Department of State, the Department of Homeland Security, and other executive departments and agencies that are consulted.

13803.s: This order revives the National Space Council and lets it resume operations. The Council advises and assists the President on national space policy and strategy, reviews U.S. space policy, develops recommendations, and monitors how the policy is carried out. It includes several Cabinet officials and other senior officials, and it can also convene a non-Federal Users' Advisory Group.

13804.s: This order gives more time before parts of Executive Order 13761 take effect by changing several July 12, 2017 dates to October 12, 2017. It also revokes section 11 of Executive Order 13761. The order says it is meant to allow more fact-finding and a more complete review of the Government of Sudan's actions.

13805.s: This order creates a Presidential Advisory Council on Infrastructure in the Department of Commerce. The council is to study federal funding, support, and delivery of infrastructure projects and make findings and recommendations to the President. It also looks at ways to speed up approvals, improve financing, increase public-private partnerships, and improve procurement and grant procedures.

13806.s: This order directs the government to study the United States manufacturing and defense industrial base and the resiliency of supply chains tied to national security. It requires a report that identifies important goods and manufacturing capabilities, looks at risks that could disrupt supply chains, and assesses weaknesses in domestic capacity, workforce skills, and energy use. It also asks for recommended legislative, regulatory, and policy changes to help prepare for disruptions and strengthen supply chains.

13807.s: This order directs federal agencies to make environmental reviews and permit decisions for infrastructure projects coordinated, predictable, and transparent. It sets a policy to use a permitting timetable, involve the public and other levels of government early, and aim to finish federal reviews and authorization decisions for major infrastructure projects within 2 years. It also creates a process called "One Federal Decision" for major projects, with a lead federal agency and a goal of completing federal authorization decisions within 90 days after a Record of Decision. It applies to federal agencies that review, authorize, or consult on infrastructure projects and to major infrastructure projects that need multiple federal authorizations.

13808.s: This order adds sanctions tied to the situation in Venezuela. It prohibits certain transactions by U.S. persons or within the United States, including new debt, new equity, certain bonds, dividend payments, and some securities from the Government of Venezuela and PdVSA. It also bans transactions that try to evade these limits and any conspiracy to break them.

13809.s: This order revokes Executive Order 13688, which had dealt with federal support for local law enforcement equipment acquisition. It also directs executive departments and agencies to stop carrying out the recommendations made under that order and to rescind any related rules, regulations, guidelines, or policies if needed. It affects state, tribal, and local law enforcement and the federal agencies that work with them.

13810.s: This order adds sanctions related to North Korea. It blocks property and interests in property of certain people and companies tied to North Korea, limits aircraft and vessels that have been in North Korea, and allows sanctions on foreign financial institutions that do certain transactions connected to North Korea. It also suspends the entry of aliens who meet the listed criteria and bars attempts to evade the order.

13811.s: This order continues a list of federal advisory committees until September 30, 2019. It also says the head of the department or agency named for each committee will carry out the President’s functions under the Federal Advisory Committee Act for those committees. It supersedes parts of Executive Order 13708 and revokes Executive Order 13805.

13812.s: This order revokes an earlier order that created the National Council on Federal Labor-Management Relations and labor-management forums across the executive branch. It directs the Office of Personnel Management and executive agencies to rescind orders, rules, regulations, guidelines, programs, or policies that carried out that earlier order. It says existing collective bargaining agreements are not canceled.

13813.s: This order directs federal agencies to consider changes that would expand access to association health plans, short-term limited-duration insurance, and health reimbursement arrangements. It also says government rules should help people buy insurance across state lines, increase competition in healthcare markets, and improve access to price and outcome information. The order affects employers, employees, small businesses, and people looking for health insurance coverage.

13814.s: This order amends a prior order about the Ready Reserve and gives the Secretary of Defense more authority to manage personnel needs during a national emergency. It also makes certain national emergency powers under sections 688 and 690 of title 10 available to the Secretary concerned, and for the Army, Navy, and Air Force, under the direction of the Secretary of Defense. It applies in the context of the declared national emergency tied to the September 11, 2001 attacks.

13815.s: This order resumes the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program and lets the Secretary of State resume travel of qualified and appropriately vetted refugees into the United States. It says the refugee screening and vetting process has been improved and now generally meets the uniform baseline for immigration screening and vetting. The Secretary of Homeland Security and the Secretary of State must keep assessing risks from certain refugees, and the Attorney General must report on the effects of refugee resettlement on national security, public safety, and general welfare.

13816.s: This order approves a new official seal for the National Credit Union Administration. It says the seal is for the agency and describes what the design symbols mean. It also revokes the earlier order that had established a seal for the NCUA.

13817.s: This order directs the federal government to reduce the United States’ vulnerability to disruptions in the supply of critical minerals. It calls for finding new sources, increasing activity across the supply chain, improving access to topographic, geologic, and geophysical data, and streamlining leasing and permitting. It also requires a report with a strategy, progress review, and recommendations on critical minerals.

13818.s: This order blocks property and property interests in the United States for certain people tied to serious human rights abuse or corruption, including people listed in the annex and others the Treasury Secretary determines meet the order’s criteria. It also suspends the entry into the United States of aliens who meet those criteria. The order bars certain donations, contributions, and transfers of funds, goods, or services to or from blocked persons.

13819.s: This order sets new rates of basic pay for many federal pay systems, including the General Schedule, Foreign Service, Veterans Health Administration, Senior Executive Service, and certain executive, legislative, and judicial salaries. It also sets pay rates for members of the uniformed services, cadets and midshipmen, locality-based comparability payments, and administrative law judges. The new rates take effect on January 1, 2018, or at the start of the first applicable pay period after that date. It also supersedes Executive Order 13756 on the effective dates listed here.

13820.s: This order revokes Executive Order 13799 and ends the Presidential Advisory Commission on Election Integrity. It affects that commission and its work. The order also says it must be carried out under applicable law and subject to available funding.

13821.s: This order directs federal agencies to speed up requests to locate broadband facilities on federal property. It tells the General Services Administration to review and possibly revise a common application form, and it requires federal property managing agencies to use that form for these requests. Agencies must review requests quickly and report on how many applications they receive, approve, or reject.

13822.s: This order tells the Defense, Veterans Affairs, and Homeland Security secretaries to work together on the challenges faced by transitioning service members and veterans. It calls for a plan to improve access to mental health treatment and suicide prevention resources, especially during the year after discharge, separation, or retirement. It also requires a later report on progress, other needed reforms, and next steps.

13823.s: This order revokes the earlier order that had directed the closure of detention facilities at U.S. Naval Station Guantánamo Bay. It says detention operations there shall continue under applicable United States and international law, and that the United States may transport additional detainees there when lawful and necessary to protect the Nation. It also directs the Secretary of Defense to recommend policies on the disposition of people captured in connection with an armed conflict, including policies for transfers to Guantánamo Bay.

13824.s: This order revokes one earlier order and updates another to rename the council the President's Council on Sports, Fitness, and Nutrition. It directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to develop a national strategy to expand children's participation in youth sports, encourage regular physical activity, and promote good nutrition. It also establishes the council to advise the President and recommend actions to expand sports and fitness opportunities at the national, state, and local levels.

13825.s: This order amends parts of the Manual for Courts-Martial and sets rules for when those changes take effect. It says some amendments apply right away, while many changes from the Military Justice Act of 2016 apply only to cases or offenses on or after January 1, 2019. It also keeps earlier cases, charges, and punishments under the rules in effect when they began. The Secretary of Defense must issue nonbinding guidance for commanders and military lawyers on how to handle charges and specifications.

13826.s: This order creates a Federal Interagency Council on Crime Prevention and Improving Reentry. The council is directed to work on ways to prevent youths and adults from entering or reentering the criminal justice system, lower recidivism, and improve how inmates reenter communities. It must make recommendations and send reports to the President, and it revokes a 2016 presidential memorandum on rehabilitation and reintegration of formerly incarcerated individuals.

13827.s: This order prohibits U.S. people and people in the United States from dealing in certain digital currency, digital coin, or digital token issued by or for the Government of Venezuela on or after January 9, 2018. It also bars transactions that evade or try to evade those limits, and it bars conspiracies to violate them. The Secretary of the Treasury, with the Secretary of State, is authorized to issue rules and take action to carry out the order.

13828.s: This order directs federal agencies to review public assistance programs and related rules to see whether they fit its stated goals. It calls for stronger work requirements where allowed by law, fewer duplicate or ineffective programs, and clearer measures of whether programs help people find work, increase earnings, and escape poverty. It also says agencies should check that only eligible people receive benefits and should enforce laws on aliens who are not otherwise qualified and eligible. The order affects federal agencies, state, local, and tribal governments, and people who receive public assistance.

13829.s: This order creates a task force to review the operations and finances of the United States Postal Service. The task force must look at mail volume, package delivery, the universal service obligation, the USPS role in the economy, and the postal business model, workforce, operations, costs, and pricing. It must also develop recommendations for administrative and legislative reforms and report its findings to the President.

13830.s: This order gives certain military and Homeland Security officials the power to approve several military decorations in the President’s name. It covers awards such as the Distinguished Service Cross, Silver Star Medal, Legion of Merit, Distinguished Flying Cross, and several medals for heroism or service. It also sets rules for who can receive each award and lets the officials write regulations to carry out the order.

13831.s: This order creates the White House Faith and Opportunity Initiative within the Executive Office of the President. It is meant to work with faith-based and community organizations, and to help them compete for federal grants, contracts, programs, and other funding opportunities where allowed by law. It also requires agencies without a center for faith and opportunity initiatives to name a liaison to work with the Initiative.

13832.s: This order tells agencies to help military spouses get hired into competitive civil service jobs. Agencies must note military spouse hiring authority in job announcements, advertise it, and ask for applications from military spouses. The Office of Personnel Management must give guidance and information to agencies, and agencies must report each year on positions, applications, and appointments under this hiring authority.

13833.s: This order tells covered agencies to give their Chief Information Officers more direct control over information technology decisions. It says CIOs should report to agency heads, help with planning and budgeting, and approve component CIO appointments. The order also calls for more agency-wide IT consolidation, stronger cybersecurity steps, shared IT services where allowed, and new hiring authority for certain IT positions.

13834.s: This order directs executive agencies to meet energy and environmental requirements in a cost-effective way. It tells agencies to reduce building energy use, water use, waste, and greenhouse gas emissions, and to track and report progress. It also requires each agency to name a Chief Sustainability Officer and sets duties for federal officials to oversee and report on implementation.

13835.s: This order prohibits certain transactions related to the Government of Venezuela. It bars U.S. persons or people in the United States from buying Venezuelan government debt, dealing in some debt used as collateral after the order takes effect, or selling, transferring, assigning, or pledging certain equity interests owned by the Venezuelan government. It also forbids transactions that evade these rules and any conspiracy to violate them.

13836.s: This order directs federal agencies to seek collective bargaining agreements that support effective and efficient government, reduce costs, and preserve management rights. It creates an interagency labor relations working group to help agencies share information, develop model ground rules, and review bargaining issues that affect more than one agency. Agencies are directed to set bargaining goals, prepare reports on current agreements before they expire, and try to keep negotiations on a shorter timeline.

13837.s: This order tells executive branch agencies to limit and track taxpayer-funded union time. It says employees should spend most of their paid time doing agency work, and agencies should require advance written approval before using taxpayer-funded union time unless rules allow otherwise. It also bars employees from using that time for some activities, sets reporting and monitoring rules, and applies disciplinary action for unauthorized use.

13838.s: This order exempts certain contracts and contract-like agreements for seasonal recreational services and seasonal recreational equipment rental on federal lands from Executive Order 13658’s minimum wage rules. It still keeps those wage rules for lodging and food services linked to seasonal recreational services. Agencies must update contracts, regulations, and guidance to match the exemption.

13839.s: This order directs federal agencies to make it easier to remove employees for unacceptable performance or misconduct, while still recognizing employee procedural rights and protections. It says agencies should use Chapter 75 removal procedures in appropriate cases, may not require progressive discipline in every case, and should generally avoid longer periods to show acceptable performance unless needed. It also limits certain grievance procedures, protects information in personnel files, and requires agencies to report data on adverse actions to the Office of Personnel Management.

13840.s: This order sets federal policy for ocean, coastal, and Great Lakes waters. It creates an interagency Ocean Policy Committee to coordinate agencies, advise the President, and help manage ocean-related matters, including public release of unclassified data and support for ocean research. It also says agencies should work with states, tribal and local governments, marine industries, and other stakeholders. The order revokes Executive Order 13547.

13841.s: This order directs immigration officials to keep alien families in custody together during criminal improper entry or immigration proceedings, when allowed by law and available resources. It says families should not be held together if there is a concern that a child’s welfare would be at risk. It also directs the Attorney General to seek a change to the Flores settlement and to prioritize cases involving detained families.

13843.s: This order moves administrative law judge positions into Schedule E of the excepted service. It says these appointments will no longer be subject to the competitive hiring rules and examinations, and that agencies may use their own regulations and practices to make these appointments. Current administrative law judges who were already in the competitive service on July 10, 2018, stay in that service as long as they remain in their current positions.

13844.s: The order tells the Attorney General to create a Task Force on Market Integrity and Consumer Fraud within the Department of Justice. The task force is meant to help investigate and prosecute fraud cases involving the government, financial markets, and consumers, including cyber-fraud and fraud targeting the elderly, service members, veterans, and other members of the public. It also replaces the earlier Financial Fraud Enforcement Task Force.

13845.s: This order creates the President's National Council for the American Worker and an advisory board to help develop a national strategy on education and job training for American students and workers. The council is told to make recommendations on workforce policy, apprenticeship and work-based learning, access to job data, and ways to improve training and retraining. It also directs agencies to work with employers, schools, labor unions, and state, local, tribal, and territorial governments on these issues.

13846.s: This order reimposes sanctions on people and foreign financial institutions that do business with Iran in certain areas. It targets support for the Government of Iran’s purchase of U.S. bank notes or precious metals, dealings with certain Iranian persons, and activity in Iran’s energy, shipping, shipbuilding, automotive, petroleum, and petrochemical sectors. It also allows visa denial or exclusion from the United States for some corporate officers, principals, or controlling shareholders of a sanctioned person.

13847.s: The order sets a federal policy to expand access to workplace retirement plans for American workers. It directs the Secretary of Labor and the Secretary of the Treasury to review rules on multiple employer plans, retirement plan notices and disclosures, and required minimum distribution tables. It also looks at ways to help small and mid-sized businesses, part-time workers, sole proprietors, working owners, and other workers with non-traditional employer-employee relationships.

13848.s: This order declares a national emergency over foreign interference in United States elections. It requires government officials to assess possible foreign interference after an election and report on its effects on election infrastructure, voting, or campaign-related systems. It also blocks property and interests in property of foreign persons involved in such interference, and it can suspend their entry into the United States.

13849.s: This order directs federal agencies to help carry out sanctions under CAATSA and the Ukraine Freedom Support Act against persons selected by the President, the Secretary of State, or the Secretary of the Treasury. It can block property, limit loans and foreign exchange transactions, restrict exports and government contracts, and deny visas or entry to certain people connected to the sanctioned person. It also bars actions that evade these sanctions.

13850.s: This order blocks property and property interests in the United States for certain people tied to Venezuela’s gold sector, corruption, support for blocked persons, or ownership and control by blocked persons. It also suspends their entry into the United States as immigrants or nonimmigrants. The order bars donations, contributions, and transactions that try to evade these restrictions.

13851.s: This order declares a national emergency over the situation in Nicaragua. It blocks property and interests in property in the United States of certain people linked to human rights abuse, actions against democratic processes or institutions, threats to peace or stability, corruption, or support for blocked persons. It also suspends the entry into the United States of aliens who meet those criteria, unless the Secretary of State finds their entry is in the national interest.

13852.s: This order closed all executive departments and agencies of the Federal Government on December 5, 2018, as a mark of respect for George Herbert Walker Bush. Agency heads could keep some offices open and require some employees to report if needed for national security, defense, or other public need. It also says that date counts under certain pay and leave rules for federal employees.

13853.s: This executive order creates the White House Opportunity and Revitalization Council. The Council is meant to coordinate federal efforts to encourage public and private investment in urban and economically distressed communities, including qualified opportunity zones. It also reviews ways to reduce regulatory burdens, support economic growth, and improve access to federal resources. The order requires reports to the President with recommended changes to laws, rules, policies, and programs.

13854.s: This order closes all executive departments and agencies of the Federal Government on Monday, December 24, 2018, and excuses their employees from duty. Agency heads may keep certain offices or employees open if needed for national security, defense, or other public need. It also says December 24, 2018, counts under laws and orders about federal employee pay and leave.

13855.s: This order directs the Interior and Agriculture Departments to manage federal forests, rangelands, and other federal lands to reduce wildfire risk and improve land conditions. It calls for shared fire management priorities, faster agency processes, and more use of tools like prescribed burns, mechanical thinning, and unmanned aerial systems. It also directs the departments to work with states, tribes, local governments, communities, non-profit organizations, and the private sector on restoration, road access, and fuel reduction.

13856.s: This order sets new basic pay rates and salary ranges for several federal pay systems, including the General Schedule, Foreign Service, Veterans Health Administration, Senior Executive Service, Executive Schedule, Vice President, Congress, justices and judges, uniformed services, and administrative law judges. It also sets locality-based comparability payments and directs the Office of Personnel Management to carry out and publish those payments. The order says the new pay schedules take effect on the dates listed in the order and supersede a prior order.

13857.s: This order takes additional steps related to the national emergency with respect to Venezuela. It changes the definition of the “Government of Venezuela” to include the state and government of Venezuela, its political subdivisions, agencies, and instrumentalities, including the Central Bank of Venezuela and PDVSA, as well as people owned or controlled by them or acting for them, including members of the Maduro regime. It applies to actions involving the Venezuelan government and people connected to it.

13858.s: This order directs executive departments and agencies that run certain covered programs to encourage people getting new federal financial assistance awards to use goods, products, and materials produced in the United States. It applies to contracts, subcontracts, purchase orders, and sub-awards tied to infrastructure projects, including iron, aluminum, steel, cement, and other manufactured products. It also requires agencies to report ways they can increase the use of U.S.-produced materials and changes Executive Order 13788 to use the term "Federal financial assistance" instead of "Federal grants."

13859.s: This order directs federal agencies to make artificial intelligence a priority in research, data access, technical standards, and workforce training. It tells agencies to look for ways to increase access to federal data and computing resources for AI research while protecting safety, privacy, and confidentiality. It also calls for guidance on AI-related regulations and for plans to support reliable and trustworthy AI systems. The order affects federal agencies, AI researchers, workers, and industries that use AI.

13860.s: This order directs the Defense and Homeland Security departments to identify military training and experience that may count toward merchant mariner credentials. It also calls for actions on fee waivers or fee payments for active duty service members, payment for Transportation Worker Identification Credential cards, and prompt certification of sea service after discharge or release. The order also tells the United States Committee on the Marine Transportation System to support merchant mariner credentialing and report yearly to the President.

13861.s: This order directs the creation of a plan to reduce veteran suicide and improve veterans’ quality of life. It sets up a task force made up of several cabinet officials and asks it to develop a roadmap, a local grant proposal, and a national research strategy. The plan would focus on coordination across federal, state, local, tribal, private, and nonprofit groups, and on services for veterans and their families.

13862.s: This order revokes a reporting requirement in Executive Order 13732. That earlier requirement called for an annual unclassified summary of U.S. strikes against terrorist targets outside areas of active hostilities and assessments of deaths from those strikes. The order does not change the separate reporting requirements in the National Defense Authorization Acts for Fiscal Years 2018 and 2019.

13863.s: This order updates the definition of a “significant transnational criminal organization” under a prior executive order. It says such a group must include one or more foreign persons, take part in serious criminal activity across at least two foreign states or one foreign state and the United States, and threaten U.S. national security, foreign policy, or economy. It affects executive departments and agencies carrying out the order under existing law and available funding.

13864.s: This order directs federal agencies to help colleges and universities support free inquiry and open debate on campus. It also requires the Education Secretary to create a secure website and mobile app for federal student loan borrowers and to expand the College Scorecard with more data on earnings, debt, default rates, and repayment rates. The order also requires reports on sharing student loan risk, reforming default collections, and ways to help students finish degrees faster and at lower cost.

13865.s: This order directs federal agencies to coordinate work on protecting the nation from electromagnetic pulses, or EMPs. It requires agencies to identify critical functions and critical infrastructure that could be badly affected, review test data, and develop plans to improve resilience, response, and recovery. It also calls for information sharing with private-sector partners and for annual reports, risk assessments, and research on EMP effects.

13866.s: This order adjusts pay rates for several federal pay systems, including the General Schedule, Foreign Service, Veterans Health Administration, Senior Executive Service, executive branch salaries, Congress, judges, uniformed services, locality-based payments, and administrative law judges. It also directs the Office of Personnel Management to help carry out the locality-based payments and publish notice in the Federal Register. The new schedules take effect on the dates listed in the order, and it supersedes an earlier executive order.

13867.s: This order changes how presidential permits are handled for certain cross-border facilities and land transportation crossings at the international boundaries of the United States. It directs the Secretary of State to receive applications, gather needed views and information, and advise the President, but the President makes the final decision to issue, deny, or amend a permit. It covers facilities like pipelines, water or sewage export or import facilities, transportation facilities, bridges when congressional approval is not required, and border crossings for motor and rail vehicles. It also revokes two prior executive orders on this subject, while existing permits stay in effect unless changed by the proper authority.

13868.s: This order directs federal agencies to promote private investment in energy infrastructure by speeding up permitting, reducing duplicate reviews, and updating related guidance and rules. It also directs reviews of Clean Water Act water quality certifications, LNG safety rules, and whether LNG may be transported in approved rail tank cars. The order requires reports on barriers to moving energy resources, the use of federal authorities to support energy development, and ways to promote economic growth in the Appalachian region. It also calls for reviews of retirement plan energy investments and proxy voting guidance, and for work on renewing expired energy rights-of-way.

13869.s: This order transfers the main responsibility for background investigations from the Office of Personnel Management to the Department of Defense. It makes the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency the primary federal entity for these investigations and gives it duties for classified access, Defense Department jobs, contractor work, and other federal suitability or fitness checks. It also directs the Department of Defense and the Office of Personnel Management to carry out the transition, move support functions and resources, and report on the transfer until it is complete.

13870.s: This order directs federal agencies to strengthen the cybersecurity workforce and improve training, mobility, and recognition for cybersecurity workers. It calls for a rotational assignment program, use of the NICE Framework in contracts and personnel programs, and a list of aptitude assessments to help identify employees for reskilling. It also directs agencies to recognize cybersecurity and cyber-operations achievements and develop an annual cybersecurity competition for federal civilian and military employees. It asks agencies to work on plans and reports about national cybersecurity workforce needs and skills gaps.

13871.s: This order blocks property and property interests of people involved in Iran’s iron, steel, aluminum, or copper sectors, and of people who do significant business tied to those sectors. It also allows sanctions on foreign financial institutions that knowingly handle significant transactions for those sectors or for blocked persons. The order bans certain donations, limits contributions and services to or from blocked persons, and suspends entry into the United States for people who meet the listed criteria.

13872.s: This order creates a Presidential Advisory Commission and a White House Initiative for Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders. They are meant to broaden access to economic resources and opportunities for AAPI employers and communities and to advise on Federal programs related to that access. They also will work on research, data collection, and analysis about AAPI populations, subpopulations, and businesses.

13873.s: This order declares a national emergency over risks from foreign adversaries in information and communications technology and services. It bans certain transactions involving those technologies or services when they are tied to a foreign adversary and are found to pose risks to national security, critical infrastructure, the digital economy, or the safety of United States persons. The Secretary of Commerce is given authority to carry out the order, set rules, and allow some transactions with risk-mitigation measures. Other agencies must help with assessments and reports on these threats.

13874.s: This executive order sets a policy for federal oversight of agricultural biotechnology products that is based on science, risks, and public health and environmental protection. It directs Agriculture, the Environmental Protection Agency, and the Food and Drug Administration to review and streamline regulations, and to consider exempting low-risk products from undue regulation. It also calls for a shared web platform, public outreach, and international strategies to increase acceptance of these products and support U.S. agricultural exports.

13875.s: This order tells executive departments and agencies to review their current advisory committees and terminate at least one-third of certain committees by September 30, 2019, unless a waiver is granted. It also limits the government-wide total of eligible committees to 350 and restricts new ones if that limit is exceeded. Agencies must also send reports and plans about whether committees should continue or be ended. Merit review panels and advisory committees that mainly provide scientific expertise for product safety or effectiveness are exempt.

13876.s: This order blocks property and interests in property in the United States of the Supreme Leader of Iran, the Supreme Leader's Office, and certain other people tied to them. It also lets the Treasury Department sanction foreign financial institutions that knowingly do significant financial business for those blocked people. The order suspends entry into the United States of aliens who meet certain listed criteria and bans transactions that try to evade these rules.

13877.s: This order directs federal agencies to push hospitals and other healthcare providers to make price and quality information easier for patients to see and compare. It also asks for steps to give patients more information about expected out-of-pocket costs before they get care and to help protect them from surprise medical bills. The order calls for better quality reporting across several federal health programs and for more access to de-identified claims data for researchers and others, while protecting patient privacy and security.

13878.s: This order creates a White House Council on Eliminating Regulatory Barriers to Affordable Housing. The council is set up to work with federal, state, local, tribal, and private sector leaders to find and reduce rules and practices that raise housing development costs and limit housing supply. It affects agencies and officials involved in housing policy, and it is meant to support renters, homeowners, developers, and others connected to housing.

13879.s: This order directs the Health and Human Services Secretary to launch an awareness effort on kidney disease, develop proposals for research, and share information with patients and providers. It also orders new payment models to test ways to identify at-risk patients earlier, increase home dialysis and kidney transplants, and support care for Medicare beneficiaries with kidney disease. The order calls for steps to encourage artificial kidneys, improve organ matching and delivery, and remove financial barriers for living organ donation.

13880.s: The order directs all agencies to give the Department of Commerce the maximum help allowed by law in collecting records that can be used to determine the number of citizens, non-citizens, and illegal aliens in the country. It also creates an interagency working group to improve access to administrative records and asks Commerce to consider ways to expand citizenship data collection in the future. The information is to be used only to produce statistics and not for immigration enforcement against particular individuals.

13881.s: This order directs federal agencies to maximize the use of goods, products, and materials produced in the United States when they buy for the government, as allowed by law. It tells the FAR Council to consider new rules for when materials count as foreign origin and to review the price rules used to decide whether a foreign bid is unreasonable or against the public interest. It also says the head of each executive agency should issue rules needed to match any final rule.

13882.s: This order blocks property and interests in property of people the Treasury Secretary finds are involved in certain actions tied to Mali. It also suspends their entry into the United States as immigrants or nonimmigrants, unless the Secretary of State decides their entry is in the national interest. The order applies to people linked to threats to Mali’s peace and security, attacks on civilians and security forces, obstruction of humanitarian aid, trafficking, corruption, and support for blocked persons.

13883.s: This order sets rules for carrying out certain sanctions against a country when the President or the Secretary of State selects them under the Chemical and Biological Weapons Control and Warfare Elimination Act. It directs the Treasury Department, with the State Department, to oppose some international financial assistance and to bar U.S. banks from making loans or giving credit to that country, except for food or other agricultural goods. It also forbids transactions or conspiracies that try to evade those loan and credit bans.

13884.s: This order blocks property and interests in property of the Government of Venezuela that are in the United States or under the control of a United States person. It also blocks property of certain people the Treasury Secretary determines have helped blocked persons or are owned or controlled by them. The order suspends the entry into the United States of aliens who meet those criteria, with some exceptions, and bans transactions that try to evade these restrictions.

13885.s: This order creates the National Quantum Initiative Advisory Committee. The committee will advise the Secretary of Energy and the National Science and Technology Council subcommittee on quantum information science and technology, and it will make recommendations when the National Quantum Initiative Program is reviewed and revised. Its members are to come from industry, universities, federal laboratories, and other federal agencies, and it may also gather information from other stakeholders.

13886.s: This order revokes Executive Order 12947 and amends Executive Order 13224 on terrorism sanctions. It blocks property and property interests of certain listed people and foreign persons tied to terrorism, and it allows the Treasury Department to restrict some foreign financial institutions that handle significant transactions for blocked persons. It also keeps the rules subject to laws, regulations, and licenses issued under the order.

13887.s: This order directs federal agencies to modernize the domestic influenza vaccine system. It calls for less reliance on egg-based vaccine production, more use of faster and more scalable manufacturing methods, and development of vaccines that can protect against many or all influenza viruses. It also creates a task force to make a 5-year plan and report on ways to increase influenza vaccination and improve public understanding.

13888.s: This order says refugees should be resettled only in places where both state and local governments have given written consent, with some limited exceptions. It directs the Secretary of State and the Secretary of Health and Human Services to create a process to check that consent and to release written consents publicly. If a state or locality does not consent, refugees should not be resettled there unless the Secretary of State finds an exception applies. The rule does not apply to a refugee’s spouse or child following to join that refugee.

13889.s: This order continues a list of federal advisory committees until September 30, 2021. The committees include groups on the White House, science, trade, labor, health, veterans, education, and several national monuments. It also says the head of each named department or agency will carry out the President’s functions for those committees under the Federal Advisory Committee Act.

13890.s: This executive order directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to propose changes to Medicare that would give beneficiaries more plan choices and improve access to providers, including through telehealth and network changes. It also calls for steps to reduce regulatory burdens, encourage innovation, and improve how Medicare pays for care. The order says the administration will work to protect Medicare, combat fraud, waste, and abuse, and preserve Social Security retirement insurance benefits for seniors who choose not to receive Medicare Part A.

13891.s: This order tells executive branch agencies to treat guidance documents as non-binding, except where law or a contract makes them binding. It requires agencies to keep a searchable online database of guidance documents, review them, and rescind ones they decide should no longer be in effect. It also requires agencies to set procedures for issuing guidance, including public notice and comment for significant guidance documents and clear statements that the guidance does not bind the public.

13892.s: This order tells federal agencies to act more transparently and fairly in civil administrative enforcement and adjudication. It says agencies must give prior public notice of the standards and jurisdiction they rely on, avoid using guidance documents to add new conduct standards, and give people a chance to respond before an action with legal consequences in most cases. It also requires some agencies to publish inspection rules, follow paperwork rules for information requests, and report on compliance with SBREFA. The order does not apply to certain foreign, military, national security, homeland security, or criminal matters, and it does not create a right that can be enforced in court.

13893.s: This order tells executive branch agencies to consider the budget effects of some administrative actions before taking them. If an agency wants to do an action that would increase mandatory spending, it must also propose other action to reduce mandatory spending, unless the Director of OMB waives the requirement. It applies to discretionary administrative actions by agencies and covers proposed rules, programs, notices, and guidance that affect mandatory spending.

13894.s: This order blocks property and interests in property of certain people connected to the situation in Syria, including some current or former Turkish officials, Turkish government entities, and others who meet listed criteria. It also allows sanctions against foreign people who obstruct a ceasefire, block displaced people from returning home, force people or refugees back to Syria, or interfere with efforts for a political solution. The order suspends entry into the United States for certain people covered by these criteria, unless the Secretary of State makes an exception. It also can affect foreign financial institutions that knowingly handle significant transactions for blocked persons.

13895.s: This order establishes the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, or PCAST. The council advises the President on science, technology, education, and innovation policy, and can provide scientific and technical information on public policy for the economy, workers, national and homeland security, and other topics. It also requires executive departments and agencies to provide information when requested, and it revokes a prior executive order on the same council.

13896.s: This order directs the Attorney General to establish a Commission on Law Enforcement and the Administration of Justice. The Commission will study law enforcement and criminal justice issues and make recommendations on ways to prevent, reduce, and control crime, increase respect for the law, and assist victims. It may invite State, local, and tribal officials to serve, and it may also gather input from law enforcement agencies, public health experts, victims rights organizations, businesses, nonprofit groups, and others with relevant experience.

13897.s: This order revokes Executive Order 13495, which had required some successor Federal contractors to offer a right of first refusal of employment to employees under the earlier contract. It also tells the Secretary of Labor, the Federal Acquisition Regulatory Council, and executive departments and agencies to rescind rules and policies that implemented or enforced that order. The Secretary of Labor must end any investigations or compliance actions based on Executive Order 13495.

13898.s: This order creates a federal task force on missing and murdered American Indians and Alaska Natives. The task force is led by the Attorney General and the Secretary of the Interior, and it includes other federal officials. It must consult with tribal governments, develop model protocols for new and unsolved cases, review cold cases, and issue reports to the President.

13899.s: This order says the executive branch will enforce Title VI against discrimination rooted in anti-Semitism as strongly as it enforces other Title VI discrimination cases. It tells agencies enforcing Title VI to consider the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance definition of anti-Semitism and its examples when looking for evidence of discrimination based on race, color, or national origin. It also tells agency heads to report other nondiscrimination authorities where that definition could be considered.

13900.s: The order closes all executive departments and agencies of the federal government on December 24, 2019, and excuses their employees from duty that day. Agency heads may keep some offices or employees working for national security, defense, or other public need, and the order also covers how pay and leave rules apply to federal employees.

13901.s: This order sets new basic pay rates and salaries for several federal pay systems, including the General Schedule, Foreign Service, Veterans Health Administration, Senior Executive Service, executive, legislative, and judicial salaries. It also sets pay rates for members of the uniformed services, cadets and midshipmen, locality-based comparability payments, and administrative law judges. Most of the schedules take effect on the first applicable pay period on or after January 1, 2020, and the uniformed services pay schedule takes effect January 1, 2020.

13902.s: This order blocks property and interests in property in the United States for certain people linked to sectors of the Iranian economy, including construction, mining, manufacturing, and textiles, as well as others who help them. It also lets the Treasury Department sanction foreign financial institutions that knowingly handle significant financial transactions connected to those sectors or to blocked persons. The order suspends the entry into the United States of people who meet these criteria, with some exceptions, and it exempts transactions for agricultural commodities, food, medicine, and medical devices to Iran.

13903.s: This order directs federal agencies to focus on preventing human trafficking and the online sexual exploitation of children. It calls for more prosecution of offenders, help for victims, and prevention education. It also sets steps for agencies to improve coordination, share resources online, and work with schools and other groups to support victims and fund prevention programs.

13904.s: This order directs the government to target e-commerce shipments that bring contraband into the United States or avoid customs duties, taxes, and fees. It sets new rules for importer of record numbers and says people suspended or debarred by CBP for import or trade violations cannot get one while that status lasts. It also directs agencies to work with postal services, carriers, customs brokers, and e-commerce platforms to track noncompliant international posts, publish certain violation information, and report on fees and enforcement.

13905.s: This order says the Federal Government should promote the responsible use of positioning, navigation, and timing services to protect critical infrastructure. It directs several agencies to develop PNT profiles, test weaknesses in critical infrastructure, and create contract language for Federal contracts that use these services. It also calls for a national plan for new PNT services that do not depend on global navigation satellite systems and for a source of Coordinated Universal Time that does not depend on GNSS.

13906.s: This order changes the membership of the National Space Council and says the Vice President chairs it. It also revokes the quarterly reporting requirement in Executive Order 13803. The order applies to the council, its members, and the executive departments, agencies, and officials named in it.

13907.s: This order creates the Interagency Environment Committee for Monitoring and Enforcement. The committee is set up to coordinate U.S. efforts to monitor and enforce environmental obligations under the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement Implementation Act, including work related to Mexico and Canada. It also has members from several federal departments and agencies, with the United States Trade Representative serving as chair.

13908.s: This order creates an interagency committee to give advice on how to carry out and change parts of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement that deal with automotive goods. The committee will review the agreement’s rules of origin, the alternative staging regime, and the effect of new technology, and it will look at the economic effects on the United States economy, workers, and consumers. It also directs the Secretary of the Treasury, the Secretary of Labor, and the Commissioner of U.S. Customs and Border Protection to issue regulations and other measures needed to implement section 202A.

13909.s: This order gives the Secretary of Health and Human Services authority over the nationwide priority and allocation of health and medical resources needed to respond to COVID-19 in the United States. It covers resources such as personal protective equipment and ventilators, and it lets the Secretary identify other health and medical resources that meet the legal criteria. The Secretary may also control the distribution of these materials in the civilian market and issue rules needed to carry out the order.

13910.s: This order says health and medical resources needed to respond to COVID-19 should not be hoarded. It gives the Secretary of Health and Human Services authority to prevent hoarding and to set rules about certain scarce materials. It also lets the Secretary gather information about how these supplies are distributed and decide when a designation is no longer needed.

13911.s: This order gives the Secretaries of Health and Human Services and Homeland Security added authority under the Defense Production Act to respond to the spread of COVID-19 in the United States. It lets them help expand domestic production of health and medical resources, including personal protective equipment and ventilators, and use powers for loans, purchases, priorities, and allocation. It also allows voluntary agreements and plans of action by private businesses to help produce and distribute these resources.

13912.s: This order gives the Secretaries of Defense and Homeland Security authority to order Selected Reserve units and certain Ready Reserve members to active duty for the COVID-19 national emergency. It allows them to call up units or members for up to 24 consecutive months, with no more than 1,000,000 members on active duty at one time. It applies to reserve members under the Secretary concerned and says state officials must be consulted for National Guard Reserve Component units activated under this authority.

13913.s: This order creates a committee to help the Federal Communications Commission review foreign participation in the United States telecommunications services sector. The committee reviews applications and existing licenses for risks to national security and law enforcement interests. It can recommend denying, conditioning, modifying, or revoking a license, or taking no action. The order also sets out how the committee can ask for information and share certain information with other government entities.

13914.s: This order says the United States should encourage international support for the public and private recovery and use of resources in outer space, including water and certain minerals. It directs the Secretary of State to oppose treating the Moon Agreement as customary international law. It also directs the Secretary of State to seek joint statements and other agreements with foreign states about safe and sustainable space resource operations.

13915.s: This order sets the line of succession for the Secretary of the Interior if both the Secretary and Deputy Secretary have died, resigned, or are unable to serve. It lists which Interior officials would act in that role, in order, starting with the Solicitor of the Department of the Interior. It also says no one serving in one of those jobs in an acting capacity may become Secretary under this order, and it revokes Executive Order 13244.

13916.s: This order gives the Secretary of the Treasury authority to consider temporarily extending deadlines for certain estimated payments during the COVID-19 national emergency. It applies to importers who are suffering significant financial hardship because of COVID-19, except for certain payments assessed under listed sections of U.S. law. The Secretary must consult with the Secretary of Homeland Security or a designee before using this authority.

13917.s: This order gives the Secretary of Agriculture authority over food supply chain resources, including meat and poultry, during the COVID-19 national emergency. It directs the Secretary to take action to keep meat and poultry processors operating and to help make sure the supply of those products continues. It also lets the Secretary identify other food supply chain resources that fit the law and issue orders and rules to carry out the order.

13918.s: This order creates an Interagency Labor Committee to coordinate U.S. efforts to monitor Canada and Mexico’s labor obligations and Mexico’s labor reform. The committee may also recommend enforcement actions with respect to Canada or Mexico under the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement Implementation Act. It includes representatives from several federal departments and agencies, and the Department of Labor provides funding for the required hotline.

13919.s: This order directs the Secretary of Defense to call certain Selected Reserve units and individual members to active duty. It allows up to 200 Selected Reservists at any one time for up to 365 consecutive days. The activation is for the named mission called the "Enhanced Department of Defense Counternarcotic Operation in the Western Hemisphere."

13920.s: This order declares a national emergency about threats to the United States bulk-power system. It prohibits certain acquisitions, imports, transfers, or installations of bulk-power system electric equipment when the equipment is tied to a foreign adversary and the Secretary of Energy finds it poses certain risks. It also creates a task force to develop federal energy procurement policies and to report on its work. The order defines the bulk-power system and the equipment covered by its rules.

13921.s: This order directs federal agencies to reduce barriers for American fishing and aquaculture and to support seafood production. It calls for actions to fight illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing, including new rulemaking and more training and technical assistance. It also directs agencies to speed up environmental reviews and permits for aquaculture projects, identify suitable areas for commercial aquaculture, and publish guidance on aquaculture rules and grant programs.

13922.s: This order gives the Chief Executive Officer of the United States International Development Finance Corporation authority under the Defense Production Act. The authority may be used for loans and other actions to create, maintain, protect, expand, or restore domestic industrial base capabilities and domestic supply chains needed to respond to the COVID-19 outbreak. It applies to strategic resources and supply chains within the United States and its territories.

13923.s: This order creates the Forced Labor Enforcement Task Force to monitor United States enforcement of the prohibition in section 307 of the Tariff Act of 1930. The task force is chaired by the Secretary of Homeland Security and includes representatives from several federal departments and the Office of the United States Trade Representative. It must try to decide actions by consensus, and if needed, by majority vote. Each department and agency pays its own expenses related to the task force.

13924.s: This executive order tells federal agencies to use emergency powers and other available tools to support economic recovery from COVID-19. It directs agencies to look for regulations and requirements that may slow recovery and consider rescinding, modifying, waiving, or exempting people or businesses from them when allowed by law. It also tells agencies to speed up guidance for regulated people and businesses, consider enforcement discretion, and review temporary rule changes to see which ones might be made permanent.

13925.s: This order says online platforms should not restrict protected speech and directs federal agencies to review how they spend advertising money on those platforms. It also directs the Commerce Department, Justice Department, and FTC to take steps related to section 230, unfair or deceptive acts, and complaints about online censorship. The Attorney General must also set up a working group on state enforcement and develop a proposal for federal legislation.

13926.s: This order directs the State Department and USAID to put international religious freedom into foreign policy and foreign aid planning. It also tells agencies to budget at least $50 million a year for programs that advance religious freedom, unless law and funding limits prevent it. The order requires training for certain federal employees and asks agencies to use diplomacy and, in some cases, economic tools or sanctions in countries where religious freedom is violated.

13927.s: This order tells federal agencies to use their emergency and other legal powers to speed infrastructure investments and other actions that can help the economy recover from the COVID-19 emergency. It directs the Secretary of Transportation, the Secretary of the Army, and certain other Cabinet agencies to expedite authorized and appropriated projects on highways, civil works, Federal lands, and other infrastructure projects. It also tells agencies to use emergency procedures, statutory exemptions, categorical exclusions, and other NEPA and Endangered Species Act processes to move projects forward, while still following applicable law and protecting public health, safety, natural resources, and the environment.

13928.s: This executive order declares a national emergency over efforts by the International Criminal Court to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute United States personnel or personnel of certain allied countries without consent. It blocks property and interests in property of certain foreign persons involved in those efforts or who support them. It also suspends the entry of those people, their immediate family members, and some ICC officials, employees, and agents into the United States, with limited exceptions.

13929.s: This order directs the Attorney General to set standards for independent credentialing of state and local law enforcement agencies and to tie some Justice Department grant funding to that process. It also directs the creation of a database on excessive use of force and certain officer actions, and it requires some public reporting from that database. The order tells federal officials to develop training and support for law enforcement encounters involving impaired mental health, homelessness, and addiction, and to propose new legislation and grant program changes.

13930.s: This order directs federal officials to improve the child welfare system and reduce the need to place children in foster care. It calls for more data, stronger partnerships with public, private, faith-based, and community groups, and more support for caregivers, guardianship, kinship care, and older youth. It also requires guidance on adopting and foster care placements, including equal treatment under the Multiethnic Placement Act and rights of parents and children with disabilities.

13931.s: This order continues the President's National Council for the American Worker and the American Workforce Policy Advisory Board. The Council and the Board are extended until September 30, 2021, unless the President extends the Council again. The order says it must be carried out under applicable law and subject to available appropriations.

13932.s: This order directs federal agencies to review and revise job classification and qualification standards for competitive service jobs. It says agencies should base job postings on the skills and competencies needed for the job, and may require education only when it is legally required or directly tied to the job. It also requires agencies to use hiring assessments that do not rely only on education or self-evaluations. The changes apply to federal competitive service hiring.

13933.s: This order says the federal government should prosecute people or groups that damage, deface, or destroy monuments, memorials, statues, government property, or religious property. It also says the government should prosecute people or groups that incite violence or illegal activity connected to those riots and acts of vandalism. It directs agencies to review grant programs and withhold some federal support from state and local governments and law enforcement agencies that fail to protect public monuments and statues. It also allows certain federal departments to provide personnel to help protect federal monuments, memorials, statues, or property.

13934.s: This order creates an interagency task force to plan a National Garden of American Heroes, a public statuary park. The task force must report on possible locations and ways to create the garden, and it should consider statues of historically significant Americans. It also tells federal agencies to prioritize commissioning public statues and artworks of historically significant Americans and to support programs that teach about the founding documents and founding ideals of the United States.

13935.s: This order creates a White House Hispanic Prosperity Initiative in the Department of Education. The initiative is meant to improve Hispanic Americans' access to educational and economic opportunities by promoting practices, partnerships, and federal programs that support those goals. It also creates an interagency working group and a presidential advisory commission to help advise on issues affecting Hispanic Americans.

13936.s: This order says the United States will suspend or end different treatment for Hong Kong in ways allowed by law. It suspends the application of several immigration, export, and trade provisions that had treated Hong Kong differently from China, and it directs agencies to take steps such as changing regulations, ending certain agreements, and stopping some programs. It also blocks property of certain foreign persons tied to actions in Hong Kong, bars donations to them, and suspends their entry into the United States, along with some immediate family members and agents.

13937.s: This order directs the Department of Health and Human Services to act so some future grants are tied to health centers making insulin and injectable epinephrine available at the price the center paid, plus a small administration fee. It applies to low-income people who have high cost sharing, a high unmet deductible, or no health insurance. The policy is meant to help Americans without affordable access to these medications through commercial insurance or federal programs.

13938.s: This order directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to take steps to expand safe access to lower-cost imported prescription drugs. It allows waivers of the prohibition on importing prescription drugs when there is no added public safety risk and costs go down for American patients. It also authorizes re-importation of insulin products for emergency medical care and calls for rulemaking to allow importation of certain prescription drugs from Canada.

13939.s: This order directs the Health and Human Services Secretary to finish rulemaking on prescription drug discounts in Medicare Part D. It seeks to move certain drug rebates away from health plan sponsors, pharmacies, and pharmacy benefit managers and toward patients at the point of sale. It also calls for new safe harbors for point-of-sale discounts and certain PBM service fees, while confirming the action will not increase federal spending, Medicare premiums, or patients' total out-of-pocket costs.

13940.s: This order tells executive departments and agencies to review certain Federal contracts and hiring practices from fiscal years 2018 and 2019. It looks at the use of temporary foreign labor, offshoring work done in the United States, and whether agency employment policies follow citizenship requirements for Federal employment. It also directs the Secretaries of Labor and Homeland Security to take action to protect United States workers from adverse effects on wages and working conditions caused by H-1B visa holders at job sites.

13941.s: This order directs the government to improve rural health care and telehealth access. It tells the Secretary of Health and Human Services to announce a new payment model for rural health care providers, and it directs HHS and the Secretary of Agriculture to develop a strategy to improve rural health infrastructure. It also calls for a report on ways to increase rural access to care, reduce maternal mortality and morbidity, and improve mental health, and it tells HHS to review telehealth and other Medicare flexibilities that were used during the public health emergency.

13942.s: This order directs that certain transactions with ByteDance Ltd. and its subsidiaries be prohibited 45 days after the order, if allowed by law. It also says that transactions by a United States person or within the United States that evade or try to evade the ban are prohibited. The Secretary of Commerce must identify the transactions covered by the ban and may issue rules to carry it out.

13943.s: This order says certain transactions related to WeChat with Tencent Holdings Ltd. and its subsidiaries are prohibited 45 days after the order, to the extent allowed by law. It also bars transactions that try to evade or violate those limits, including conspiracies to do so. The Secretary of Commerce is directed to identify the transactions covered and may issue rules to carry out the order.

13944.s: This order directs federal agencies to increase domestic procurement of essential medicines, medical countermeasures, and critical inputs. It also tells agencies to look for supply chain weaknesses, and it directs health officials, the Food and Drug Administration, and the Department of Defense to identify vulnerabilities and make lists of products that are needed. The order calls for steps to support domestic production, streamline certain regulatory requirements, and give priority to federal contracts for these products when needed.

13945.s: This order tells federal agencies to look at temporary steps to stop some residential evictions and to review ways to prevent evictions and foreclosures linked to COVID-19 hardships. It also directs officials to find federal funds for temporary help for renters and homeowners who are struggling to pay rent or mortgages. The order affects renters, homeowners, tenants, landlords, public housing authorities, affordable housing owners, and recipients of federal grant funds.

13946.s: This order changes federal space rules so that, when federal space needs are being met, preference is given to qualified opportunity zones, other distressed areas, and centralized community business areas when allowed by law and by cost and security needs. It also changes rules for locating federal facilities on properties in central cities to use the term "distressed communities" and to refer to qualified opportunity zones, other distressed areas, and centralized business districts. The changes apply to the Administrator of General Services and to federal departments and agencies that work on federal space and facility location.

13947.s: This order directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to take steps to test a payment model for certain high-cost prescription drugs and biological products covered by Medicare Part B. Under that model, Medicare would pay no more than the most-favored-nation price, which is the lowest price a drug manufacturer sells that product for in a comparable OECD country. It affects Medicare Part B patients and taxpayers who help pay for those drugs.

13948.s: This order says Medicare should not pay more than the most-favored-nation price for certain costly prescription drugs and biological products in Part B and Part D. It directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to take steps to test payment models that would use that price. It also revokes the earlier executive order on lowering drug prices.

13949.s: This order blocks property and interests in property of certain people linked to the supply, sale, transfer, or support of arms and related materiel to or from Iran. It also suspends the entry into the United States of aliens who meet those criteria, unless the Secretary of State decides otherwise. The order does not apply to certain transactions for agricultural commodities, food, medicine, or medical devices, or to official U.S. or United Nations business.

13950.s: This order says the United States should not promote race or sex stereotyping or scapegoating in the federal workforce or the Uniformed Services, and it says federal grant funds should not be used for those purposes. It bars the Uniformed Services from teaching certain “divisive concepts” and says service members cannot be penalized for refusing to accept them. It also requires government contractors to stop using workplace training that teaches those concepts, to notify workers and unions, and it directs the Labor Department to set up a hotline and investigate complaints.

13951.s: This executive order lays out a healthcare plan focused on patient choice, lower costs, and more transparent prices and quality information. It says the plan affects patients, Medicare beneficiaries, doctors, hospitals, insurers, employers, and states. It also says people with pre-existing conditions should continue to have access to affordable health insurance and care.

13952.s: This order directs the Department of Health and Human Services to make sure federally funded programs follow federal laws protecting infants born alive, including premature infants and infants with disabilities. It says hospitals and other programs must provide an appropriate medical screening exam, stabilizing treatment, or transfer when needed, and must not unlawfully discourage parents from seeking treatment for a disabled infant. It also directs the department to investigate complaints, take enforcement action for violations, and prioritize funding for research and training related to life-saving treatment for these infants.

13953.s: This order says the United States should reduce its reliance on critical minerals from foreign adversaries and strengthen domestic mining and processing. It directs the Interior Secretary and other agencies to study that reliance, report to the President, and recommend actions that may include tariffs, quotas, or other import restrictions. It also tells agencies to expand secure mineral supply chains, review research and funding needs, and consider ways to support mining and processing projects in the United States.

13954.s: This order directs federal agencies to help prevent suicide, drug-related deaths, and poor mental and behavioral health outcomes, especially those made worse by COVID-19 shutdown orders. It creates a Coronavirus Mental Health Working Group to review mental-health needs, including for minorities, seniors, veterans, small business owners, children, people with disabilities, and people with a substance use disorder. It also tells agencies to look at grant programs that support in-person and telehealth treatment, support groups, group therapy, and community activities, including religious services.

13955.s: This order creates a United States One Trillion Trees Interagency Council. The council will coordinate federal work on tree growing, restoration, and conservation, and it will work with key stakeholders and with the One Trillion Trees initiative. It also tells federal agency heads to include council work in planning and to report progress on tree-related activities. The council will end on December 31, 2030.

13956.s: This order directs federal agencies that work on water matters to coordinate more closely on water storage, water quality, water infrastructure, forecasting, and related programs. It creates an interagency Water Subcabinet to identify overlapping working groups and recommend ways to reduce duplication and improve planning. It also calls for recommendations on water supply reliability, drought resilience, water systems, water data, and training and retaining water-sector workers.

13957.s: This order creates Schedule F in the excepted service for Federal jobs that are confidential, policy-determining, policy-making, or policy-advocating and are not normally changed during a Presidential transition. It directs agencies to review covered positions and may place some existing or new positions into Schedule F. It also says agencies must set rules to prohibit the personnel practices barred by section 2302(b) for Schedule F employees and applicants.

13958.s: This order creates the President's Advisory 1776 Commission in the Department of Education. The commission is to study the history and principles of the American founding, make a report to the President, and advise on patriotic education and other related activities. It also directs agencies to monitor compliance with Constitution Day requirements and to prioritize federal resources for patriotic education in certain programs.

13959.s: This order blocks United States persons from buying or selling certain publicly traded securities tied to Communist Chinese military companies and related securities. It also allows limited transactions for divesting holdings during set time periods. The Secretary of the Treasury and other agencies are directed to carry out the order and may issue rules and licenses.

13960.s: This order directs federal agencies to use artificial intelligence in ways that are lawful, accurate, safe, understandable, transparent, and accountable. It says agencies should use AI to improve government operations and services while protecting privacy, civil rights, civil liberties, and American values. It also requires agencies to inventory their non-classified and non-sensitive AI use cases and share those inventories with other agencies and, when practicable, the public.

13961.s: This order directs executive departments and agencies to keep the ability to carry out key government functions under all conditions and to build continuity and risk management into day-to-day operations. It also creates a Federal Mission Resilience Executive Committee to help carry out a new strategy for the executive branch and to review and coordinate continuity policy. The order changes the designation of the National Continuity Coordinator and revokes part of Executive Order 13618, with those responsibilities moved to the new committee.

13962.s: This order directs federal officials to make safe and effective COVID-19 vaccines available to Americans. It says Americans should have priority access to free vaccines, and that the most vulnerable U.S. populations should get first access. After enough doses are available for Americans who choose to be vaccinated, it directs officials to help other countries get access to these vaccines.

13963.s: This order sets the line of succession for the Secretary of Defense if the Secretary dies, resigns, or cannot do the job. It lists Department of Defense officials who would act as Secretary in a set order, and it says some acting officials and some people not appointed with Senate consent cannot serve under this order. It also revokes a 2010 executive order on the same subject.

13964.s: This order directs the government to brand United States foreign assistance as “American aid” and use a single logo on related materials, goods, packaging, and public communications. It applies to foreign assistance under the Foreign Assistance Act and other laws, including humanitarian assistance and disaster relief programs, with some exceptions and waivers for safety, security, or other concerns. It also requires agencies to update or remove any rules that conflict with this directive and to report on implementation.
